explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is a static educational website (HTML5/CSS3 course materials).
   - Purpose: host PDFs, code samples (HTML/CSS exercises), and challenges for learners.
   - Hosted via GitHub Pages, no dynamic backend.

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top‐level:
     • _config.yml indicates a Jekyll/GitHub Pages build.
     • aulas-pdf: PDFs of lectures.
     • exercicios: folders of HTML/CSS exercises.
     • desafios: PDF challenges and supporting files.
     • imagens: site images (e.g., mascote.png).
   - README.md describes site content and links.
   - .gitignore, LICENSE—standard repo files.

3. Extract insights from README
   - Static site with direct links to PDFs and live HTML demos.
   - Uses GitHub Pages URL structure (gustavoguanabara.github.io/html-css).

4. Main components for the system design diagram
   a. Content authoring environment
      – Developer’s local machine (editor, Git CLI).
   b. Source code repository
      – GitHub repo (branches, commits).
   c. Build pipeline
      – Jekyll (reads _config.yml, converts any markdown to HTML).
   d. Hosting platform
      – GitHub Pages (serves static assets over HTTPS/CDN).
   e. End user
      – Learner’s web browser (requests HTML/CSS/PDF files).

5. Relationships and data flow
   - Author edits files → commits to Git → push to GitHub.
   - GitHub triggers Pages build via Jekyll → outputs static site.
   - GitHub Pages CDN serves content → browser requests/receives assets.
   - Browser renders HTML/CSS; PDFs open via built‐in viewer or download.

6. Architectural patterns/design principles
   - Static site generator (Jekyll) pattern.
   - Content‐pipeline separation: raw assets (PDFs), templates, final output.
   - Infrastructure as code: configuration (_config.yml) controls build.

7. Technologies/frameworks/libraries
   - Git/GitHub for version control and hosting.
   - Jekyll (built into GitHub Pages) for static site generation.
   - HTML5/CSS3 for front‐end.
   - PDF assets as binary resources.

8. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram
   - Draw distinct layers:
     1) Content layer (source files, PDFs, images, HTML/CSS).
     2) Build layer (Jekyll).
     3) Hosting layer (GitHub Pages).
     4) Client layer (user browser).
   - Show directional arrows:
     • Local → GitHub (push).
     • GitHub → Build (Jekyll).
     • Build → Hosting (deploy).
     • Browser ← Hosting (fetch).
   - Color‐code layers:
     • Blue for authoring/dev.
     • Green for build/deployment.
     • Orange for hosting/CDN.
     • Gray for end user.

9. Diagramming elements to include
   - Clear boxes labeled:
     • “Developer Local” (VSCode, Git CLI)
     • “GitHub Repo” (main branch)
     • “Jekyll Build” (via _config.yml)
     • “GitHub Pages” (CDN endpoint)
     • “Browser” (Chrome/Firefox)
   - Arrows with verbs: push, build, deploy, request, serve.
   - Use distinct shapes or colors for:
     • Static assets folder (aulas-pdf, exercicios, desafios).
     • Configuration file.
     • Build engine.
     • CDN/hosting.

10. Emphasis on detail
    - Represent each major directory as a sub‐component in the content box.
    - Label the build step explicitly as “Jekyll SSG”.
    - Highlight that no dynamic backend or database exists.
    - Show that PDFs and images are served identically to HTML/CSS assets.
    - Capture the continuous deployment nature of GitHub Pages.

By following these steps, you will produce a precise, clear system design diagram reflecting the static‐site architecture, its content pipeline, and hosting workflow. Ensure all labels, arrows, and color codes are consistent to aid quick comprehension.
